name: Giant Component
miniText: The scientific question is whether random edge addition creates a sharp change in large-scale reachability. In NetLogo's Giant Component model, initially isolated nodes receive uniformly selected new edges, and connected components merge as the graph becomes denser. The selected literature connects this mechanism to random-network connectivity: finite random graphs exhibit the birth of a giant component [1]; network structure determines component and reachability properties [2]; rewired local networks offer a contrasting connectivity mechanism [3]. Finite-size fluctuations, undirected edges and uniform mixing restrict extrapolation to structured human contacts. The original NetLogo behavior is the baseline for reimplementation. This simulation offers a controlled thought experiment, and agreement with its output does not establish empirical validation.

The work Watts describes was originally published in: P. Erdos and A. Renyi. On random graphs. Publ. Math. Debrecen, 6:290-297, 1959. This paper has some additional analysis: S. Janson, D.E. Knuth, T. Luczak, and B. Pittel. The birth of the giant component. Random Structures & Algorithms 4, 3 (1993), pages 233-358.

verification.evidenceSummary: AbstractLimiting distributions are derived for the sparse connected components that are present when a random graph on n vertices has approximately 1/2n edges. In particular, we show that such a graph consists entirely of trees, unicyclic components, and bicyclic components with probability approaching √2/3 cosh √5/18 ≈ 0.9325 as n→∞. The limiting probability that it is consists of trees, unicyclic components, and at most one another component is approximately 0.9957; the limiting probability that it is planar lies between 0.987 and 0.9998. When a random graph evolves and the number of edges passes 1/2n, its components grow in cyclic complexity according to an interesting Markov process whose asymptotic structure is derived. verification.evidenceSummary: Abstract. Inspired by empirical studies of networked systems such as the Internet, social networks, and biological networks, researchers have in recent years developed a variety of techniques and models to help us understand or predict the behavior of these systems. Here we review developments in this field, including such concepts as the small-world effect, degree distributions, clustering, network correlations, random graph models, models of network growth and preferential attachment, and dynamical processes taking place on networks.
